claims.claim: When provided alone and above 10 µM, spermidine strongly decreased c-di-GMP reporter activity.
claims.source: When provided alone and above a concentration of 10 µM, norspermidine and spermidine strongly increased and decreased, respectively, c-di-GMP reporter activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Norspermidine increased the c-di-GMP reporter output by ~60% relative to WT.
claims.source: At the limit, relative to the WT, norspermidine increased the c-di-GMP reporter output by ~60% while spermidine reduced reporter output by ~25%.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results based on the c-di-GMP reporter data.

claims.claim: Spermidine reduced the c-di-GMP reporter output by ~25% relative to WT.
claims.source: At the limit, relative to the WT, norspermidine increased the c-di-GMP reporter output by ~60% while spermidine reduced reporter output by ~25%.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results based on the c-di-GMP reporter data.

claims.claim: When norspermidine is present above 50 µM, it overrides the effect of exogenous spermidine, irrespective of spermidine concentration.
claims.source: Notably, consistent with previous end-point biofilm assays, when norspermidine was present above 50 µM, it overrode the effect of exogenous addition of spermidine, irrespective of spermidine concentration (Figure 3C; McGinnis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3C, consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: V. cholerae cytoplasmic c-di-GMP levels are responsive to extracellular blends of polyamines.
claims.source: Thus, V. cholerae cytoplasmic c-di-GMP levels are responsive to extracellular blends of polyamines.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the c-di-GMP reporter data with polyamine mixtures.

claims.claim: When norspermidine is abundant, V. cholerae produces high levels of c-di-GMP, matrix expression is increased, and biofilms do not disperse.
claims.source: When norspermidine is abundant, V. cholerae produces high levels of c-di-GMP, matrix expression is increased, and biofilms do not disperse.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined biofilm lifecycle, vpsL-lux, and c-di-GMP reporter data.

claims.claim: When spermidine is abundant and norspermidine is absent or below threshold, V. cholerae c-di-GMP levels drop, matrix production is repressed, and biofilm dispersal occurs.
claims.source: In contrast, when spermidine is abundant and norspermidine is absent or present below a threshold concentration, V. cholerae c-di-GMP levels drop, matrix production is repressed, and biofilm dispersal occurs.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined biofilm lifecycle, vpsL-lux, and c-di-GMP reporter data.

claims.claim: The ΔmbaA mutant was impervious to the addition of norspermidine or spermidine with only modest reductions in biofilm biomass.
claims.source: To our surprise, the ΔmbaA mutant was impervious to the addition of either polyamine as both polyamines caused only a very modest reduction in overall biofilm biomass, and dispersal timing resembled the untreated ΔmbaA control (Figure 3D, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claims.claim: Titration of polyamines onto the ΔmbaA strain carrying the c-di-GMP reporter did not substantially alter reporter output.
claims.source: Consistent with this result, titration of the polyamines alone and in combination onto the ΔmbaA strain carrying the c-di-GMP reporter did not substantially alter reporter output (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The dynamic response of WT V. cholerae to polyamines requires MbaA.
claims.source: These results show that the dynamic response of WT to polyamines requires MbaA.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of response to polyamines in the ΔmbaA mutant.

claims.claim: The minor reduction in biofilm production in the ΔmbaA mutant when supplied polyamines is likely due to non-specific effects, perhaps via interaction with negatively charged matrix components.
claims.source: We suspect that the minor reduction in biofilm production that occurred in the ΔmbaA mutant when supplied polyamines is due to non-specific effects, perhaps via interaction of polyamines with negatively charged matrix components.
claims.evidence: This is presented as speculation to explain the minor effects observed.

claims.claim: In the absence of NspS, MbaA is thought to function as a constitutive phosphodiesterase.
claims.source: In the absence of its partner polyamine binding protein, NspS, MbaA is thought to function as a constitutive phosphodiesterase (Cockerell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Deletion of nspS in WT V. cholerae reduced peak biofilm biomass by 65% and dispersal initiated 4 hr earlier than in WT.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, deletion of nspS in an otherwise WT strain reduced overall peak biofilm biomass by 65% and dispersal initiated 4 hr prior to when dispersal begins in the WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the ΔnspS mutant, c-di-GMP levels were lower than in WT, showing that MbaA is locked as a constitutive phosphodiesterase.
claims.source: In the ΔnspS mutant, c-di-GMP levels were lower than in the WT as judged by the c-di-GMP reporter (Figure 3F), showing that MbaA is locked as a constitutive phosphodiesterase.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Exogenous addition of polyamines to the ΔnspS mutant had no effect on c-di-GMP levels.
claims.source: Exogenous addition of polyamines had no effect on c-di-GMP levels (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The WT V. cholerae response to polyamines is controlled by the NspS-MbaA polyamine sensing circuit.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that the WT V. cholerae response to polyamines is controlled by the NspS-MbaA polyamine sensing circuit.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined data on ΔmbaA and ΔnspS mutants.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic domain of MbaA exhibits phosphodiesterase but not diguanylate cyclase activity in vitro.
claims.source: The cytoplasmic domain of MbaA exhibits phosphodiesterase but not diguanylate cyclase activity in vitro (Cockerell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: When an intact regulatory domain is present, MbaA could possess both phosphodiesterase and diguanylate cyclase activities.
claims.source: We reasoned that, when an intact regulatory domain is present, MbaA could possess both enzymatic activities, with the activity of each domain inversely controlled by NspS binding.
claims.evidence: This is presented as reasoning/hypothesis to be tested.

claims.claim: Tagging MbaA with 3xFLAG did not alter MbaA control over the biofilm lifecycle.
claims.source: To ensure that our mutations did not destabilize MbaA, we first fused MbaA to 3xFLAG and introduced the gene encoding the fusion onto the chromosome at the mbaA locus. Tagging did not alter MbaA control over the biofilm lifecycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 2.

claims.claim: The E553A substitution (EVL*) did not alter MbaA-3xFLAG abundance.
claims.source: To inactivate the MbaA phosphodiesterase activity, we substituted the conserved catalytic residue E553 with alanine, converting EVL to AVL (referred to as EVL* henceforth). This change did not alter MbaA-3xFLAG abundance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: V. cholerae harboring MbaAEVL* exhibited an increase in biofilm biomass and a strong biofilm dispersal defect.
claims.source: V. cholerae harboring MbaAEVL* exhibited an increase in biofilm biomass and a strong biofilm dispersal defect (Figure 4A), and only a modest response to exogenous polyamines, with norspermidine eliciting some inhibition of biofilm dispersal and spermidine driving a small reduction in overall biofilm biomass (Figure 4B, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4A, B and Video 2.

claims.claim: Treatment with norspermidine increased c-di-GMP levels in V. cholerae carrying MbaAEVL*, albeit not to the level of WT.
claims.source: Treatment with norspermidine did increase c-di-GMP levels in V. cholerae carrying MbaAEVL* as judged by the reporter output (Figure 4C), albeit not to the level of WT (Figure 3C), suggesting that the V. cholerae mbaAEVL* mutant, which is incapable of c-di-GMP degradation, retains the capacity to synthesize some c-di-GMP via the MbaA SGDEF domain.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The V. cholerae mbaAEVL* mutant retains the capacity to synthesize some c-di-GMP via the MbaA SGDEF domain.
claims.source: Treatment with norspermidine did increase c-di-GMP levels in V. cholerae carrying MbaAEVL* as judged by the reporter output (Figure 4C), albeit not to the level of WT (Figure 3C), suggesting that the V. cholerae mbaAEVL* mutant, which is incapable of c-di-GMP degradation, retains the capacity to synthesize some c-di-GMP via the MbaA SGDEF domain.
claims.evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the c-di-GMP reporter data.

claims.claim: The V. cholerae mbaAEVL* strain displayed little reduction in c-di-GMP levels in response to spermidine, presumably because it lacks the phosphodiesterase activity required to degrade c-di-GMP.
claims.source: In contrast, the V. cholerae mbaAEVL* strain displayed little reduction in c-di-GMP levels in response to spermidine, presumably because it lacks the phosphodiesterase activity required to degrade c-di-GMP (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: MbaA is capable of synthesizing c-di-GMP in vivo in the presence of norspermidine.
claims.source: Thus, despite the fact that the purified cytoplasmic domain functioned only as a phosphodiesterase in vitro, our results suggest that, in vivo, MbaA is capable of synthesizing c-di-GMP in the presence of norspermidine.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MbaAEVL* mutant data showing c-di-GMP synthesis in response to norspermidine.

claims.claim: The D426A and E427A substitutions (SGDEF*) did not affect MbaA protein levels.
claims.source: To validate this prediction, we altered the conserved catalytic residues D426 and E427 to alanine residues, yielding the inactive MbaA SGAAF variant (referred to as SGDEF*). These substitutions did not affect protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The mbaASGDEF* mutant behaved identically to the ΔmbaA mutant.
claims.source: In every regard, the mbaASGDEF* mutant behaved identically to the ΔmbaA mutant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results based on comparison of phenotypes.

claims.claim: The V. cholerae mbaASGDEF* mutant exhibited a modest biofilm dispersal defect.
claims.source: The V. cholerae mbaASGDEF* mutant exhibited a modest biofilm dispersal defect (Figure 4A) and biofilm biomass was reduced in response to exogenous norspermidine and spermidine (Figure 4D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4A, D and Video 2.

claims.claim: Addition of polyamines to the mbaASGDEF* mutant harboring the c-di-GMP reporter did not drive substantial changes in reporter output.
claims.source: Furthermore, addition of polyamines to the mbaASGDEF* mutant harboring the c-di-GMP reporter did not drive substantial changes in reporter output (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The MbaA SGDEF domain is indispensable for the MbaA response to polyamines.
claims.source: These results show that the MbaA SGDEF domain is indispensable for the MbaA response to polyamines.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mbaASGDEF* mutant data.

claims.claim: The MbaA phosphodiesterase and diguanylate cyclase domains are both required for MbaA to respond properly to polyamines to regulate V. cholerae biofilm dispersal.
claims.source: Based on the results in Figures 3 and 4, we conclude that the MbaA phosphodiesterase and diguanylate cyclase domains are both required for MbaA to respond properly to polyamines to regulate V. cholerae biofilm dispersal.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the combined data from Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: Elevated periplasmic norspermidine levels drive NspS to bind to MbaA, suppressing MbaA phosphodiesterase activity and activating diguanylate cyclase activity, leading to c-di-GMP accumulation and commitment to the biofilm lifestyle.
claims.source: We propose a model in which elevated periplasmic norspermidine levels drive NspS to bind to MbaA. Consequently, MbaA phosphodiesterase activity is suppressed and the diguanylate cyclase activity dominates, which leads to c-di-GMP accumulation and commitment to the biofilm lifestyle (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is presented as a model based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: When spermidine is detected or periplasmic polyamine concentrations are low, NspS dissociates from MbaA, MbaA diguanylate cyclase activity is suppressed, phosphodiesterase activity dominates, leading to reduced c-di-GMP and favoring biofilm dispersal.
claims.source: In contrast, when spermidine is detected, or when periplasmic polyamine concentrations are low, NspS dissociates from MbaA. Consequently, MbaA diguanylate cyclase activity is suppressed and its phosphodiesterase activity dominates, which leads to a reduction in cytoplasmic c-di-GMP and favors biofilm dispersal (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is presented as a model based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Addition of norspermidine did not alter the non-dispersing phenotype of the ΔpotD1 mutant.
claims.source: Addition of norspermidine did not alter the non-dispersing phenotype of the ΔpotD1 mutant, whereas spermidine treatment drove premature biofilm dispersal and a reduction in peak biofilm biomass (Figure 5A, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A and Video 1.

claims.claim: Spermidine treatment of the ΔpotD1 mutant drove premature biofilm dispersal and a reduction in peak biofilm biomass.
claims.source: Addition of norspermidine did not alter the non-dispersing phenotype of the ΔpotD1 mutant, whereas spermidine treatment drove premature biofilm dispersal and a reduction in peak biofilm biomass (Figure 5A, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A and Video 1.

claims.claim: Addition of norspermidine to the ΔpotD1 strain did not alter the c-di-GMP reporter output.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, addition of norspermidine to the ΔpotD1 strain did not alter the c-di-GMP reporter output, whereas addition of spermidine reduced output signal, but only at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Addition of spermidine to the ΔpotD1 strain reduced c-di-GMP reporter output, but only at the highest concentrations tested.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, addition of norspermidine to the ΔpotD1 strain did not alter the c-di-GMP reporter output, whereas addition of spermidine reduced output signal, but only at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: PotD1-mediated import is not required for spermidine to modulate the biofilm lifecycle.
claims.source: These biofilm lifecycle and reporter results show that PotD1-mediated import is not required for spermidine to modulate the biofilm lifecycle.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ΔpotD1 mutant's response to spermidine.

claims.claim: Endogenously produced norspermidine is secreted into the periplasm in V. cholerae.
claims.source: Thus, we considered an alternative mechanism to underlie the V. cholerae ΔpotD1 phenotype. We hypothesized that endogenously produced norspermidine is secreted into the periplasm.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to explain the ΔpotD1 phenotype.

claims.claim: In WT V. cholerae, the equilibrium between norspermidine release and PotD1-mediated reuptake places MbaA into a partially liganded state with modest net phosphodiesterase activity.
claims.source: In the case of WT V. cholerae, the equilibrium between norspermidine release and PotD1-mediated reuptake places MbaA into a partially liganded state, and as a consequence, MbaA exhibits modest net phosphodiesterase activity (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the ΔpotD1 mutant, periplasmic norspermidine levels become elevated, NspS detects norspermidine, binds to MbaA, and promotes the MbaA diguanylate cyclase active state.
claims.source: In the V. cholerae ΔpotD1 mutant that cannot reimport norspermidine, we predict that periplasmic norspermidine levels become elevated, NspS detects norspermidine, binds to MbaA, and promotes the MbaA diguanylate cyclase active state (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is presented as a prediction/hypothesis and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In the ΔpotD1 mutant, c-di-GMP is synthesized and biofilm dispersal is prevented due to elevated periplasmic norspermidine.
claims.source: In the V. cholerae ΔpotD1 mutant that cannot reimport norspermidine, we predict that periplasmic norspermidine levels become elevated, NspS detects norspermidine, binds to MbaA, and promotes the MbaA diguanylate cyclase active state (Figure 5D). Hence, c-di-GMP is synthesized and biofilm dispersal is prevented.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a prediction/hypothesis and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In the absence of norspermidine biosynthesis, NspS would remain unliganded and MbaA would function as a constitutive phosphodiesterase.
claims.source: If this hypothesis is correct, norspermidine biosynthesis would be a requirement for biofilm formation because in the absence of norspermidine production, NspS would remain unliganded and MbaA would function as a constitutive phosphodiesterase (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is presented as a prediction based on the hypothesis and shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The ΔnspC mutant that lacks norspermidine synthesis failed to form biofilms.
claims.source: Indeed, and consistent with previous results, the ΔnspC mutant that lacks the carboxynorspermidine decarboxylase enzyme NspC that is required for norspermidine synthesis failed to form biofilms (Figure 5F; Lee et al., 2009; McGinnis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5F, consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: The ΔnspC ΔpotD1 double mutant failed to form biofilms, showing that endogenous norspermidine biosynthesis is required for the ΔpotD1 mutation to exert its effect.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ΔnspC ΔpotD1 double mutant also failed to form biofilms, showing that endogenous norspermidine biosynthesis is required for the ΔpotD1 mutation to exert its effect (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The ΔmbaA mutation is epistatic to the ΔpotD1 mutation.
claims.source: Consistent with these interpretations, the ΔmbaA mutation is epistatic to the ΔpotD1 mutation as the ΔmbaA ΔpotD1 double mutant exhibited a dispersal phenotype indistinguishable from the single ΔmbaA mutant (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Administration of exogenous norspermidine or spermidine to the ΔmbaA ΔpotD1 double mutant resulted in essentially no response.
claims.source: Administration of exogenous norspermidine or spermidine to the ΔmbaA ΔpotD1 double mutant (Figure 5H, Video 1) mimicked what occurred following addition to the single ΔmbaA mutant (Figure 3D): that is, essentially no response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5H and Video 1.

claims.claim: Information from externally supplied polyamines is transduced internally by MbaA and not via PotD1-mediated import.
claims.source: Thus, information from externally supplied polyamines is transduced internally by MbaA and not via PotD1-mediated import.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the epistasis and double mutant data.

claims.claim: The ΔpotA mutant exhibited the identical dispersal defect as the ΔpotD1 mutant.
claims.source: Lastly, to confirm that the observed ΔpotD1 phenotype was due to a defect in norspermidine transport, rather than a defect in periplasmic binding and sequestration of norspermidine, we deleted potA, encoding the ATPase that supplies the energy required for polyamine import through the PotABCD1 transporter (Kashiwagi et al., 2002). In the absence of PotA, PotD1 remains capable of binding polyamines, but no transport occurs. The ΔpotA mutant exhibited the identical dispersal defect as the ΔpotD1 mutant, demonstrating that transport of norspermidine, not sequestration by PotD1, is the key activity required for WT V. cholerae biofilm dispersal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: V. cholerae possesses two mechanisms to monitor its own numbers (norspermidine and CAI-1) and two mechanisms to take a census of unrelated organisms (spermidine and AI-2).
claims.source: Together, our findings suggest that V. cholerae possesses two mechanisms to monitor its own numbers (norspermidine and CAI-1) and two mechanisms to take a census of unrelated organisms in the environment (spermidine and AI-2), and it responds by remaining in the biofilm state when closely related species are in the majority and by exiting the biofilm state when the density of non-related organisms is high, presumably to escape competition/danger.
claims.evidence: This is presented as an interpretation/speculation in the Discussion based on the combined findings.

claims.claim: V. cholerae remains in the biofilm state when closely related species are in the majority and exits the biofilm state when the density of non-related organisms is high.
claims.source: Together, our findings suggest that V. cholerae possesses two mechanisms to monitor its own numbers (norspermidine and CAI-1) and two mechanisms to take a census of unrelated organisms in the environment (spermidine and AI-2), and it responds by remaining in the biofilm state when closely related species are in the majority and by exiting the biofilm state when the density of non-related organisms is high, presumably to escape competition/danger.

claims.claim: When norspermidine is present, MbaA synthesizes c-di-GMP.
claims.source: Despite previous work suggesting that MbaA functions exclusively as a phosphodiesterase and that its SGDEF domain, which possesses a serine substitution in the active site relative to the canonical GGDEF active site, is inert with respect to c-di-GMP synthesis, our data suggest that when norspermidine is present, MbaA does synthesize c-di-GMP (Figure 3C, Figure 4C), as has also been shown for other SGDEF proteins (Pérez-Mendoza et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4C.

claims.claim: Other SGDEF proteins have been shown to synthesize c-di-GMP.
claims.source: Despite previous work suggesting that MbaA functions exclusively as a phosphodiesterase and that its SGDEF domain, which possesses a serine substitution in the active site relative to the canonical GGDEF active site, is inert with respect to c-di-GMP synthesis, our data suggest that when norspermidine is present, MbaA does synthesize c-di-GMP (Figure 3C, Figure 4C), as has also been shown for other SGDEF proteins (Pérez-Mendoza et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: MbaA is likely a bifunctional protein capable of both c-di-GMP synthesis and degradation.
claims.source: Therefore, MbaA is likely a bifunctional protein capable of both c-di-GMP synthesis and degradation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The ability of MbaA to inversely alter c-di-GMP levels in response to two discrete cues coordinates polyamine signaling and enables more rapid and greater magnitude changes in c-di-GMP levels than would be achievable with two separate receptors.
claims.source: We speculate that the ability of MbaA to inversely alter c-di-GMP levels in response to two discrete cues coordinates polyamine signaling and enables more rapid and greater magnitude changes in c-di-GMP levels than would be achievable if two separate receptors existed, each harboring only a single catalytic activity and each responsive to only one polyamine.
claims.evidence: This is presented as speculation in the Discussion.

claims.claim: LuxN from Vibrio harveyi is a bifunctional receptor where the self-made agonist drives LuxN into phosphatase mode while antagonists induce LuxN to act as a kinase.
claims.source: An analogous bifunctional arrangement exists for the quorum-sensing two-component receptor LuxN from Vibrio harveyi. LuxN is an inner membrane receptor that harbors a periplasmic sensory domain responsible for detection of a self-made small molecule cue, a homoserine lactone agonist with a four-carbon acyl tail (Bassler et al., 1994). The ligand encodes species-specific information about cell population density. Competing bacterial species that co-occupy the niche in which V. harveyi resides produce similar acyl homoserine lactone signal molecules, and notably, those molecules differ only in the acyl tail length or decoration (Papenfort and Bassler, 2016). The tails of the molecules produced by the competitors usually possess more than four carbons, and they act as potent LuxN antagonists. With respect to mechanism, the self-made agonist drives LuxN into phosphatase mode while the antagonists induce LuxN to act as a kinase (Ke et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Ligand-driven alternations between opposing enzymatic activities could be an underappreciated mechanism that sensors employ to transmit species-specific and species-non-specific information into discrete changes in downstream behaviors.
claims.source: Thus, as in the MbaA circuit, binding of the different ligands to LuxN propels opposing enzymatic activities in the cytoplasm. We speculate that ligand-driven alternations between opposing enzymatic activities could be an underappreciated mechanism that sensors employ to transmit species-specific and species-non-specific information into discrete changes in downstream behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is presented as speculation in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The MbaA SGDEF and EVL domains could participate in dimerization and/or allosteric binding to c-di-GMP or other metabolites to mediate feedback regulation of the opposing MbaA activities.
claims.source: In addition to conveying information about the species composition of the vicinal community, the MbaA SGDEF and EVL domains could also participate in dimerization and/or allosteric binding to c-di-GMP or other metabolites to mediate feedback regulation of the opposing MbaA activities.
claims.evidence: This is presented as speculation in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Caulobacter crescentus CC3396 contains a non-catalytic GGDEF domain that binds GTP and allosterically activates the phosphodiesterase activity in the neighboring EAL domain.
claims.source: Parallel examples exist, here we present one: Caulobacter crescentus contains a GGDEF/EAL protein called CC3396, in which the GGDEF domain is non-catalytic but it nonetheless binds to GTP, which allosterically activates the phosphodiesterase activity in the neighboring EAL domain (Christen et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: A feedback mechanism could provide MbaA with the ability to integrate the information encoded in extracellular polyamine blends with cytoplasmic cues.
claims.source: A feedback mechanism could provide MbaA with the ability to integrate the information encoded in extracellular polyamine blends with cytoplasmic cues, such as the metabolic state of the cell or the current cytoplasmic c-di-GMP level.
claims.evidence: This is presented as speculation in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The double ligand detection capability linked to the dual catalytic activities of the NspS-MbaA circuit allows V. cholerae to distinguish between remarkably similar ligands and convey distinct information into the cell to alter the biofilm lifecycle.
claims.source: Taken together, the double ligand detection capability linked to the dual catalytic activities of the NspS-MbaA circuit allows V. cholerae to distinguish between remarkably similar ligands and, in response, have the versatility to convey distinct information into the cell to alter the biofilm lifecycle.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Four signaling pathways feed into the regulation of V. cholerae biofilm dispersal: starvation (RpoS), quorum sensing (via CAI-1 and AI-2), the DbfS/DbfR cascade, and polyamine signaling via NspS-MbaA.
claims.source: In summary, four signaling pathways have now been defined that feed into the regulation of V. cholerae biofilm dispersal: starvation (RpoS) (Singh et al., 2017), quorum sensing (via CAI-1 and AI-2) (Bridges and Bassler, 2019; Singh et al., 2017), the recently identified DbfS/DbfR cascade (ligand unknown) (Bridges et al., 2020), and through the current work, polyamine signaling via NspS-MbaA.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion, supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Integrating information from multiple stimuli into the control of biofilm dispersal endows V. cholerae with the ability to evaluate multiple features of its fluctuating environment prior to committing to dispersal.
claims.source: We propose that integrating the information contained in these different stimuli into the control of biofilm dispersal endows V. cholerae with the ability to successfully evaluate multiple features of its fluctuating environment prior to committing to the launch of this key lifestyle transition that, ultimately, impinges on its overall survival.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a proposal in the Discussion.

claims.claim: V. cholerae biofilm formation and biofilm dispersal are intimately connected to cholera disease and its transmission.
claims.source: Because V. cholerae biofilm formation and biofilm dispersal are intimately connected to cholera disease and its transmission, we suggest that deliberately controlling the biofilm lifecycle, possibly via synthetic strategies that target polyamine signal transduction via NspS-MbaA, could be a viable therapeutic strategy to ameliorate disease.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and reflects established knowledge.

claims.claim: Deliberately controlling the V. cholerae biofilm lifecycle via synthetic strategies targeting polyamine signal transduction via NspS-MbaA could be a viable therapeutic strategy to ameliorate cholera disease.
claims.source: Because V. cholerae biofilm formation and biofilm dispersal are intimately connected to cholera disease and its transmission, we suggest that deliberately controlling the biofilm lifecycle, possibly via synthetic strategies that target polyamine signal transduction via NspS-MbaA, could be a viable therapeutic strategy to ameliorate disease.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a suggestion/speculation in the Discussion.

results.result: MbaA is required for wild-type V. cholerae biofilm dispersal. Deletion of mbaA caused a mild biofilm dispersal defect with 27% biomass remaining at 16 hr, and complementation with ectopic mbaA expression restored normal dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 provide direct experimental evidence through time-lapse microscopy (Figure 2) and genetic complementation demonstrating MbaA's requirement for dispersal. The mild phenotype is quantified and reproducible across biological and technical replicates.

results.result: PotD1 both represses biofilm formation and promotes biofilm dispersal. The ΔpotD1 mutant exhibited 60% greater peak biofilm biomass than WT and nearly complete failure to disperse, with complementation driving premature dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide quantitative biofilm lifecycle data (Figure 2) and genetic complementation supporting dual roles for PotD1. The phenotype is more severe than ΔmbaA, suggesting distinct or additional mechanisms.

results.result: MbaA and PotD1 regulate biofilm dispersal by modulating cytoplasmic c-di-GMP levels. The ΔmbaA mutant showed 8% increased c-di-GMP while ΔpotD1 showed 39% increased c-di-GMP compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 use a validated fluorescent c-di-GMP reporter (Figure 2C) with appropriate controls and replicates. The magnitude of c-di-GMP changes correlates with dispersal phenotype severity, supporting the mechanistic link.

results.result: Matrix gene expression patterns correlate with dispersal phenotypes. The ΔmbaA mutant showed WT-like vpsL-lux expression while ΔpotD1 produced 10-fold more light, indicating normal and excess matrix production respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 use a vpsL-lux transcriptional reporter (Figure 2D) to link c-di-GMP levels to matrix gene expression. The correlation between reporter output and dispersal phenotypes is clear and quantified.

results.result: Norspermidine and spermidine have opposing effects on biofilm dispersal. Addition of 100 µM norspermidine completely prevented dispersal while 100 µM spermidine promoted premature dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 provide direct experimental evidence from time-lapse microscopy (Figure 3A, Video 1). Claims C82-C83 correctly interpret these data in the context of matrix production measurements (C80-C81), establishing opposing activities.

results.result: Norspermidine and spermidine inversely regulate matrix gene expression. vpsL-lux expression increased >10-fold with norspermidine and decreased >10-fold with spermidine treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 provide quantitative transcriptional reporter data (Figure 3B) showing dramatic opposing effects. The >10-fold changes are substantial and support the mechanism linking polyamines to matrix production.

results.result: V. cholerae cytoplasmic c-di-GMP levels respond to extracellular polyamine blends. Above 10 µM, norspermidine increased c-di-GMP reporter output by ~60% while spermidine reduced it by ~25%, with norspermidine overriding spermidine effects above 50 µM.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 use systematic titration experiments with the c-di-GMP reporter (Figure 3C) to establish dose-response relationships. The threshold concentrations and dominance hierarchy are clearly demonstrated with appropriate replicates.

results.result: The dynamic response of V. cholerae to polyamines requires MbaA. The ΔmbaA mutant was impervious to exogenous norspermidine or spermidine addition, showing no substantial changes in biofilm biomass or c-di-GMP reporter output.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 demonstrate loss of polyamine responsiveness in ΔmbaA using both biofilm lifecycle (Figure 3D) and c-di-GMP reporter assays (Figure 3E). This establishes MbaA as essential for polyamine signal transduction.

results.result: The NspS-MbaA circuit controls polyamine responses. Deletion of nspS reduced biofilm biomass by 65%, initiated dispersal 4 hr early, lowered c-di-GMP levels, and eliminated polyamine responsiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 use genetic deletion and c-di-GMP reporter assays (Figure 3F, Figure 3—supplement 1) to demonstrate NspS requirement. The phenotypes are consistent with MbaA functioning as a constitutive phosphodiesterase without NspS.

results.result: MbaA possesses diguanylate cyclase activity in vivo. The MbaAEVL* mutant (phosphodiesterase-dead) showed increased biofilm biomass, strong dispersal defects, and retained capacity to synthesize c-di-GMP in response to norspermidine but not degrade it in response to spermidine.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 use site-directed mutagenesis of the EVL domain with biofilm lifecycle and c-di-GMP reporter assays (Figure 4A-C). The data clearly demonstrate cyclase activity in vivo despite previous in vitro studies showing only phosphodiesterase activity (C101).

results.result: The MbaA SGDEF domain is indispensable for polyamine responses. The mbaASGDEF* mutant (cyclase-dead) behaved identically to ΔmbaA, showing modest dispersal defects and no substantial c-di-GMP changes with polyamine addition.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 use site-directed mutagenesis of the SGDEF domain with comprehensive phenotypic characterization (Figure 4A, D-E). The epistasis to ΔmbaA demonstrates the cyclase domain is essential for function.

results.result: Both MbaA enzymatic domains are required for proper polyamine response, with norspermidine activating cyclase activity and suppressing phosphodiesterase activity, while spermidine or low polyamine levels have opposite effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 synthesize results from domain mutation experiments (C103-C114) into a coherent model. The model is well-supported by the genetic and biochemical data showing both domains are necessary.

results.result: PotD1-mediated import is not required for spermidine to modulate biofilm dispersal. The ΔpotD1 mutant did not respond to norspermidine but spermidine still drove premature dispersal and reduced c-di-GMP at high concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 use biofilm lifecycle and c-di-GMP reporter assays with the ΔpotD1 mutant (Figure 5A-B). The differential response to the two polyamines argues against a simple import-based mechanism.

results.result: Endogenous norspermidine biosynthesis is required for the ΔpotD1 dispersal defect. Both ΔnspC and ΔnspC ΔpotD1 mutants failed to form biofilms, demonstrating norspermidine production is necessary for the ΔpotD1 phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 use genetic epistasis analysis (Figure 5F) to demonstrate norspermidine biosynthesis requirement. The double mutant phenotype clearly supports the model that accumulated endogenous norspermidine causes the ΔpotD1 defect.

results.result: Information from externally supplied polyamines is transduced by MbaA, not via PotD1-mediated import. The ΔmbaA mutation is epistatic to ΔpotD1, and the double mutant shows no response to exogenous polyamines.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 use genetic epistasis analysis (Figure 5G-H) to establish the signaling hierarchy. The epistasis clearly demonstrates MbaA functions downstream or independently of PotD1 for exogenous polyamine sensing.

results.result: Transport of norspermidine, not sequestration by PotD1, is required for WT biofilm dispersal. The ΔpotA mutant (transport-deficient but binding-competent) exhibited identical dispersal defects as ΔpotD1.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 use a clever genetic approach (Figure 5—supplement 1) to distinguish transport from binding functions. The identical phenotypes strongly support that transport, not periplasmic sequestration, is the key activity.

results.result: The ΔpotD1 dispersal defect results from elevated extracellular norspermidine accumulation due to failed reimport. Mass spectrometry showed ~25-fold more extracellular norspermidine in ΔpotD1 (2.3 µM) versus WT (90 nM), with no difference in intracellular levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C141 use quantitative mass spectrometry (Figure 5I-J) to directly measure polyamine levels. The data clearly demonstrate extracellular accumulation without biosynthesis changes, supporting the reimport failure model. Controls with ΔnspC validate the measurements.

results.result: MbaA activity remains constant throughout the biofilm lifecycle in the absence of exogenous polyamines. MbaA protein levels and intracellular polyamine concentrations did not fluctuate between biofilm formation (5 hr) and dispersal (10 hr), and extracellular norspermidine levels remained below the detection threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C148 use Western blotting and mass spectrometry (Figure 6) to measure MbaA and polyamines at two timepoints. The data support that endogenous polyamines do not drive the dispersal transition under laboratory conditions, though the limited timepoints are a weakness.

results.result: Norspermidine inhibits V. cholerae biofilm dispersal through MbaA detection in the periplasm. Norspermidine and spermidine differ by only one methylene group, yet both control dispersal via periplasmic MbaA detection and signal relay.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are supported by the combined experimental evidence showing norspermidine prevents dispersal (C78), MbaA is required for polyamine responses (C92-C94), and the structural similarity (C5) makes the discrimination remarkable.

results.result: In ΔpotD1, failure to reimport endogenous norspermidine leads to periplasmic accumulation, MbaA activation, c-di-GMP synthesis, and dispersal failure. This model explains why ΔpotD1 has more severe phenotypes than ΔmbaA.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C123-C126 present a mechanistic model supported by polyamine measurements (C135-C141), genetic epistasis (C128-C132), and c-di-GMP reporter data (C69). The model coherently explains all observations, though C123-C126 are presented as hypotheses.

results.result: V. cholerae may use polyamine sensing to distinguish 'self' from 'other' organisms. Norspermidine (rare, produced by vibrios) could signal kin presence, while spermidine (ubiquitous) could signal competitors, influencing dispersal decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C152-C159 present an attractive ecological interpretation, but this is largely speculative (C152-C156 are explicitly speculation). The low extracellular norspermidine in WT (C150) argues against canonical quorum sensing. Field studies would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: MbaA is a bifunctional enzyme capable of both c-di-GMP synthesis and degradation in vivo, despite previous in vitro studies showing only phosphodiesterase activity. Other SGDEF proteins have also been shown to synthesize c-di-GMP.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164 reconcile the current in vivo findings (C106-C109) with previous in vitro work (C101). The conclusion is well-supported by the domain mutation experiments, and C163 provides precedent from other systems.

results.result: Bifunctional enzymatic activity may enable more rapid and coordinated responses to opposing signals. This mechanism has parallels in the V. harveyi LuxN system and could allow integration of extracellular and intracellular cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C170 present interesting speculation about the advantages of bifunctionality, with C166 providing a relevant parallel from LuxN. However, these are hypotheses (C165, C167-C168, C170 are speculation) that would require additional experiments to test.

results.result: Four signaling pathways regulate V. cholerae biofilm dispersal: starvation (RpoS), quorum sensing (CAI-1 and AI-2), DbfS/DbfR, and polyamine signaling via NspS-MbaA. Integration of multiple signals allows evaluation of environmental conditions before committing to dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claim C172 summarizes established pathways with appropriate citations, including the current work on polyamines. Claim C173 is a reasonable proposal about the adaptive value of signal integration, though it remains to be experimentally tested.

results.result: Targeting polyamine signal transduction via NspS-MbaA could be a therapeutic strategy to control V. cholerae biofilm formation and dispersal, potentially ameliorating cholera disease.
results.evaluation: Claim C174 correctly notes the connection between biofilms and disease transmission. However, C175 is speculative about therapeutic applications. No drug development, in vivo infection models, or proof-of-concept experiments are presented to support this translational claim.
